# Practical Exercise: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with real-data

This exercise is useful for:

- 161.228,
- anyone who wants to practice PCA with real-data.

## Aims of this practical exercise

In this exercise you will:

- Run PCA on real-data, 
- Visualise the results,
- Interpret these results in context.

## Before you undertake this exercise...

Let’s load the packages we will need.

```{r}
library(readxl) # might need to install
library(factoextra) # might need to install
```

## Plant-based Meat Alternatives

This exercise follows the same process, and uses the same data as for PCA Example 4, blurb repeated here, for reference to the source manuscript see the lecture notes.

There are 21 different meat alternatives that they asked 140 people to assess for appearance, emotion, flavour, and texture attributes. The method of collection was choose all that apply for each set of attributes. 

In the lecture, we looked at Appearance attributes. In this practical example, we will look at Emotion attributes.

```{r}
pbma <- read_xlsx("pbma.xlsx", sheet = "Emotion attributes") 
rownames(pbma) <- pbma$option
pbma <- pbma[,2:25] # there are 25 variables, we want 2:25, because 1 is the pbma name (option)
```


## Required:

Use the `factoextra` package to perform a Principal Component Analysis for the Emotion attributes.

Make sure you:  

- consider how many PCs you want to keep and why,
- Use suitable plots to represent your PCA results,
- Use suitable numeric outputs to represent your PCA results,
- Add in "Liking" (as per the lecture demonstration) to your plots,
- Describe your findings in context,
- Provide a recommendation based on these findings.


## Solutions

You should compare your work with the [solutions for this workshop.](https://R-Resources.massey.ac.nz/practicals/pbma-sols.html)

```{r}
pbma_pca <- prcomp(pbma)
```

```{r}
summary(pbma_pca)

broom::tidy(prcomp(pbma), matrix = "pcs")
```

```{r}
screeplot(pbma_pca)

fviz_screeplot(pbma_pca)
```

need only PC1, will use PC 1 and 2

```{r}
fviz_pca_biplot(pbma_pca, repel = TRUE) + # remember the default is PC1 and PC2, repel is to stop labels overlapping
  coord_equal() # This is to make the distanecs comparable (equal) across both axes.
```

```{r}
pbma_pca$rotation
```

```{r}
sort(pbma_pca$rotation[,1])
```

```{r}
deliciousness <- read_xlsx("pbma.xlsx", sheet = "Liking")[,2] # same dataset, just a different sheet, 
# and I've just taken the Liking values using [,2]
liking <- unlist(deliciousness)
fviz_pca_ind(pbma_pca, repel = TRUE, col.ind = liking) + # colour the labels by the liking value
  coord_equal()
```

Describe your findings in context
The results are completely un-intuitive.

The pbma’s that had the highest liking (lighter blue in the plot above) mainly appear on the negative side for PC1.

The negative pole of PC1 is associated with Emotion attributes like disappointed and dissatisfied.

This is not what we’d expect. You would think that if you liked a food, you would associated it with more positive emotions.

Provide a recommendation based on these findings
Suggest the data is re-checked for accuracy, maybe some exploratory data analysis would help identify the problem.

Or, investigate potential latent variables - were these delicious foods given to consumers while a fire alarm was going off? Or in a really cold room?

Or, maybe people find food more delicious when they’re upset??

[Or maybe, because they were made up liking data, they shouldn’t follow natural intuition]
